title: Bash Examples
description: Each example belongs to one starter lesson. Follow its setup steps before trying it. These examples need the named tools and do not run in this site playground.

examples.title: Print a greeting
examples.description: printf writes formatted text. %s inserts a string and backslash-n ends the line.

examples.title: Store a text value
examples.description: A variable assignment has no spaces around equals. Dollar-name reads the value.

examples.title: Add whole numbers
examples.description: Double parentheses with a dollar sign evaluate integer arithmetic.

examples.title: Choose a message
examples.description: [[ ... ]] tests a rule. -ge means greater than or equal for whole numbers.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
score=8
if [[ "$score" -ge 5 ]]; then
 printf 'Pass\n'
else
 printf 'Try again\n'
fi

examples.title: Read an array item
examples.description: A Bash array keeps indexed values. Its first position is zero.

examples.title: Visit each value
examples.description: A for loop repeats its body for each word in a list.
examples.code:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
for n in 1 2 3; do
 printf '%s\n' "$n"
done

examples.title: Name a set of commands
examples.description: A function groups commands. $1 is its first input.

examples.title: Match a label
examples.description: case chooses commands from text patterns. ;; ends one branch.

examples.title: Use a default value
examples.description: ${name:-Guest} uses Guest when name is unset or empty.

examples.title: Count text characters
examples.description: ${#name} gives the length of the variable value.

examples.title: Read a command status
examples.description: A command returns an exit status. Zero usually means success. $? reads the last status.

examples.title: Remove a text prefix
examples.description: The # expansion removes a matching prefix from a value.
